**Verdict:** Yes. He'd have you admit your product's real flaws up front, in a sentence that ends on the claim you want believed. He calls damaging admissions possibly his favorite tactic: you give up a little promise and get more trust, and "trust trumps promise."

**Based on:** said it. He addresses this directly, for ads in the May 2025 copywriting talk and for sales calls in the February 2026 consult.

**Why they'd say it**
- He treats admissions as the strongest tool in the checklist: "nothing more powerful than damaging admissions" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 12:30, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=750s).
- The instruction is blunt: "you want to always own your flaws of course you have them of course your product isn't perfect say so" (same source, @ 12:30).
- The trade is trust for promise: "I would rather always sacrifice promise to gain trust" (@ 13:09, &t=789s).
- Your prospect is already thinking your flaws, so claiming them first costs you little: "the prospect is already thinking them" (@ 15:39, &t=939s). He tells you to "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" (@ 15:03).
- He cites research that people trust you more when you admit a bias. The vault notes the research is unnamed, so treat it as his illustration, not data.

**How to word it**
- **Put the claim after "but."** "The statement that comes after the word but is the part that is the thing you want them to believe" (@ 13:44). Order matters. He says "if I said our systems work but they're incredibly boring I'm going to emphasize on the boring part not on the fact that they work" (@ 15:03). So write "[true flaw], but [the claim]."
- **His own examples**, all in that shape:
  - "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert" (@ 15:03)
  - "our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking our AC is kind of on and off i don't have the best equipment but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's" (@ 15:39)
- **Use humor if you can.** "If you can do with humor you get even more bonus points" (@ 15:39). He also says humor is the first of his twelve ad points he'd cut, so don't force it.
- **On a sales call or long-form page, list the downsides before the benefits.** His script: "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad." (@ 19:42 in [[yt-MH-IMJxbUY4]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1182s). He frames real constraints as a trade: "So, you can have what you want, just not when you want." (@ 20:14). The point is that "they can self-qualify" (@ 20:14).

Applying his pattern to your product, with my own placeholders in place of his:
1. "[Thing buyers already complain about]. But [your core result]."
2. "[Real constraint]. If that's a dealbreaker, this isn't for you. If it isn't, [benefit]."

**Inference, not his words (confidence: medium):** every flaw he picks is true, cheap, and not the reason people buy. Ugly site, boring systems, bad parking and a bad smell all sit next to a strong core result. I'd follow that pattern and not admit a flaw that undercuts the core result. His sales-call version goes further and admits real constraints, but only to repel the wrong buyer.

**What they've done:** He opens his own talks by saying how he makes money, and he calls his sites ugly. His cited example for ad length and structure is the 12-point copy checklist, where admissions are one point among twelve. In the consult he applied front-loaded admissions to a travel-coaching offer that prospects called "too good to be true."

**What would change their answer:** It would change if the flaw is something the prospect hasn't thought of and wouldn't care about. His logic is to claim what they already suspect, so a flaw nobody suspects would only plant a doubt. He gives no test for when an admission costs sales. The vault has his examples, not a rule for that case.

Tell me your product and its top complaints and I can draft specific "flaw, but claim" lines.

**Verdict:** Alex Hormozi treats about 20% monthly churn as average for an online community and under 10% as good. He says to worry when churn reaches 30% or more, meaning fewer than 7 in 10 members stay each month. Below that line, don't chase the blended average. Look at churn by member age, because new members always churn more.

**Based on:** said it for the benchmarks and the 30% line. The cohort-based worry rule follows from what he said (confidence: medium).

**Why he'd say it**
- Average: "the platform average across School is 80% monthly retention. So said differently, it's 20% churn." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 1:39; by: hormozi; conf: high). "School" is the auto-caption for Skool, and these are Skool's platform averages. He says they apply to online and consumer services, not to insurance or alarm systems. [Video at 1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s).
- Good and bad: "the best groups have less than 10% churn, aka 90% retention month over month" and "The not good groups have less than 70% retention, aka 30% or higher." (same source, @ 1:39).
- The worry line: "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 1:39).
- Why 10% matters: moving from 20% to 10% churn means "you didn't just get a 10 or 12% boost, you got a double in the LTV per customer" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 2:13, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=133s)).
- Churn depends on how long members have been there. Months one to three run 20% or more. Then "if you keep someone 90 days, which seems to be the first kind of big churn drop-off point, it drops to around 10% or less". By month six "it goes from like 10% to 2%." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 3:53, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=233s)).
- A young community will look bad: "if your community or recurring revenue thing is less than 90 days old, then your churn is always going to be inflated" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 4:24). He adds "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks", and at 4:57: "that's normal for it to be higher than the other months, unless basically everyone's leaving, in which case, yes, you should go fix that."

**When to worry**
1. **Monthly churn is 30% or higher** (retention under 70%) in a community past its first few months. Fix retention before anything else. This is the line he stated.
2. **Cancels exceed joins.** He wants you to track both every month and "force yourself to label the businesses growing, flat, or declining" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 0:33). Declining is a leaky bucket.
3. **Churn doesn't fall with tenure.** His benchmark curve is about 20%+ in months 1–3, about 10% after day 90 and about 2% by month 6. If members past day 90 are still leaving at 20%, your problem is bigger than onboarding. He never says this exact rule; it follows from his curve.

**What he'd tell you to do**
- Get people past the first month. He calls it "the biggest month of churn" and lists activation, onboarding, expectation setting, selling the right promises and showing up every day ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 4:57).
- Day 90 needs a real outcome for the member, and month six needs them connected to other members ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 5:31). See [[business/retention/community-and-belonging]].
- Message everyone who cancels, tag the reason, and fix the top one or two every 20 cancels or so ([[business/retention/cancellation-feedback]]).
- Add a discounted annual plan: "annual always has lower churn than monthly" ([[business/retention/price-objections-and-annual-plans]]).

**What would change the answer**
- The benchmarks are Skool's own averages, and he credits Sam, Skool's founder. He sells and promotes the platform, so treat the numbers as indicative.
- Annual members make a blended churn number look better. Compare monthly payers on their own.
- The whole answer rests on one March 2026 talk. The vault has no later or earlier statement on churn rates, and `tensions.md` records no change.

**One disagreement:** Hormozi's "average" is the average across all Skool groups, not across successful ones. Calling 20% "typical" shouldn't make 20% feel acceptable. By his own numbers it's twice the churn of the best groups.

**Verdict:** Pay the $60k off, and do it in months, not years. Keep growth spending only where the return is already proven. Hormozi wouldn't hold the debt while stockpiling cash for growth. His case is about risk, not interest math.

**Based on:** he said it for the debt stance, in an almost identical case. The split between debt and growth follows from what he said (confidence: medium).

**How we get there**
1. **Nearest case.** In a live consult, ProShine's owner has exactly $60k of business debt. He plans to clear it in four to five months. Hormozi answers "Okay, good." His one argument: "debt increases risk. Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s)
2. **His ranked plan for that business.** Raise prices 10% first. Then "you're going to continue to pay off the debt. So, we're going to we're just going to keep that paid." Then fix the funnel and the ads, and only after that increase ad spend ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 30:45). The order matters. Cheap fixes come first, debt payoff is second, and extra ad spend comes last.
3. **The rule behind it.** "Safety first, so you can afford risk later" ([[thinking/hormozi]]). It shows up in three sources.

**Why he'd say it**
- He puts himself on the debt-averse side: "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37).
- He gives a reason: "businesses have seasons, they have volatility" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10). He also asks, "why did I take the, you know, the debt out to begin with? A lot of times it's like cuz I wanted to grow faster." So he doesn't treat debt-funded growth as free.
- He calls it "more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37). Paying it off is relief and safety. He doesn't present it as a big financial lever.
- The same principle shows up outside business debt: "get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible. Like do whatever you got to do to get your oxygen mask on." ([[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 17:53, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s). That quote is about personal finances, so I'm applying the principle rather than citing a debt statement.
- He would still fund growth that has a proven return: "we just want to continue to spend month over month provided our ROAS and our CAC stay more or less the same" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 10:48). In the consult, 13:1 returns justified more spend. My reading is that this comes out of operating cash flow, not new borrowing. He doesn't say how it was funded.

**What he's done:** He endorsed the ProShine payoff plan. In his own early days he banked cash for growth: "I'm going to need all this cash to open a new location, to learn more stuff, to attend more conferences" ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]] @ 13:37, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=817s). That was saved cash, and he doesn't mention borrowing in that passage.

**What would change his answer:**
- The inference is weaker if you can't clear the debt in roughly a year. ProShine does about $1.25M a year, and a four-to-five-month payoff reflects that cash flow. A much smaller business could be starved of a proven channel by a rapid payoff.
- The vault has nothing from him on interest rates. His argument is about risk, so a very cheap loan wouldn't obviously change his view, but I can't say he'd stay put.
- He isn't consistently debt-averse. He says most people take too little risk ([[yt-rMJIOK_FgJk]] @ 15:51). He also calls $200M of debt on a $100M fund the way general partners "get mega rich" ([[yt-sL16tsGafcQ]] @ 18:02). The vault logs this as an open tension in [[tensions]]. The scopes differ (private-equity structure vs. a small operating business), and he doesn't reconcile them.

**My disagreement, not his:** Paying down to zero can leave you with no cash buffer, and his own "seasons and volatility" argument cuts both ways. Keep a few months of operating cash while you pay it down.

**Verdict:** No. Raise prices, don't protect them. Your 82% close rate is the signal he reads as underpricing, not a number to defend. His plan for a duct-cleaning owner with your numbers was a 10% raise, and he said the raise only loses money if your close rate falls below about 65%.

**Based on:** said it. The vault has Hormozi's May 2026 consult with the owner of an HVAC duct-cleaning business doing about $1.25M a year. That owner had a 38% net margin and an 82% close rate. Your numbers are nearly identical, so this is the situation he already addressed.

**Why they'd say it**
- He treats 80%+ as underpriced: "So whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s))
- He rejects your premise that a higher price hurts closing: "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:00, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s))
- Underpricing can cost you the sale: "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:33). His version is that a cheap duct cleaner looks like a "super seedy duct tape operation".
- He calls this one of the biggest levers for owners under about $3–5M: "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more because people actually believe you can deliver the service now." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06)
- He gave a break-even rule: "As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06)
- He is cautious about how hard to push: "This is more asking than telling." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06) He wants incremental yardage with no Hail Marys ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 4:19).

**His numbers, checked against yours** (my arithmetic, not his words). It assumes your costs scale with the number of jobs.
- **Break-even:** a 10% raise at a 38% margin gives $0.48 profit per $1 of old price instead of $0.38. Profit holds until close rate falls to 0.82 × 0.38 / 0.48 ≈ **65%**, which matches his figure.
- **Upside:** at the same volume, a 10% raise adds about $120K on your $1.2M, which is roughly $456K to $576K in profit, or +26%. He said "roughly a 25% increase in net profit" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06).
- **Risk:** you would have to lose about 17 points of close rate before the raise costs you money. If some of your costs are fixed, the real break-even is a bit higher than 65%.

**What they've done:** At an earlier Acquisition.com workshop, his team told that same owner the business was mispriced. The owner raised prices 23% and closed more ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 6:26). Hormozi then put a further 10% raise (about $1,650 a unit) at the top of his ranked list ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 30:45, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s)).

**What would change their answer**
- **Close rate drops below break-even.** If it falls toward 65% after the raise, he'd say you've overshot. He sets that line before the raise, so you know when to roll back.
- **Veblen goods don't apply.** His argument is about trust in delivery. He explicitly separates it from luxury goods, where price itself makes the item more desirable.
- **You're short on crews.** His first question is supply or demand constraint ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 3:47). If you can't serve what you already close, a price raise would still make sense, and he'd add a priority fee for speed ([[pricing/speed-pricing/priority-fees]]). The consult owner had just added two hires and a third van.
- **He sometimes says to leave converting things alone.** In a different consult he said "The offer's already converting, so I don't really want to mess with that." ([[yt-MH-IMJxbUY4]] @ 24:06, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1446s)) That was about an ad offer in a different business. In the HVAC case he treated 82% as a reason to change price.

**One caution on the evidence:** the case rests on one consult, one owner's report of the 23% raise, and Hormozi's own framework. He sells that framework, and the vault profile notes the consult doubles as a funnel for Acquisition.com. The owner's later revenue growth came alongside a new marketing agency, so don't credit it to pricing alone. The break-even math checks out on its own, which is the part you can verify with your own numbers.

**The premise is wrong: Hormozi doesn't tell this story. The interviewer, Steven Bartlett, does.** It comes from Hormozi's Diary of a CEO interview ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]], [watch at 1:34:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5652s)). The transcript has no speaker labels, so I'm going by content. Bartlett talks about "my company" going public on a European exchange and later starting "flight story". Hormozi's own record in the vault (profile page) has no listing: he sold two-thirds of two companies to a private-equity buyer and sold a third for stock. The wiki has no page on this story either.

**What Bartlett says, between 1:34:12 and 1:37:31**
- **The NASDAQ claim:** On an IPO road show, investment banks "told me that our business would be worth four times more if it was just on a different stock market if you move it to the NASDAQ the exact same business would be worth four times more" (1:34:12). He adds that this "meant that my net worth would be Forex".
- **The lesson he drew:** A skill has to be applied in the right market. He looked for where his marketing and storytelling skills were "in least Supply but highest demand".
- **The IPO equity deal:** His pick was companies about to IPO, where a good story "can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions" (1:35:17). Rather than "help a local gym and get paid a th000 bucks", he took an equity deal with an IPO-bound company. He says the equity for 9 to 12 months of work was "worth in the region of 7 to8 million" (1:35:51).
- **The aftermath:** He founded Flight Story (about 100 people at the time of the interview) to sell the same skills into IPO-stage and biotech markets.

**What Hormozi says about it**
- **His reaction:** He treats it as a story about ignorance: "the biggest debt all of us pay is ignorance" (1:36:58; [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5818s); by: hormozi; conf: high). The vault files this under [[pricing/premium-pricing/sell-to-customers-who-value-it-most]].
- **Following up:** He gives his own version: the same conversion-rate work earns $20K for a $1M store and $2M for a $100M one, "100x same work" (1:38:38). He then tells the car-and-antique-dealer parable, whose moral is "it's not necessarily who you are but the people that value you the most" (1:40:18).
- **Calling back to it:** When he reaches capital as a type of leverage, he refers to Bartlett's story. He says "you saw like the IPO money like the fact that the NASDAQ was Forex", asks whether the exchange was "the dorf exchange", and says "there's just significantly more capital in that" market, then "same work more zeros" (1:45:47; [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6347s); by: hormozi; conf: medium). That span isn't in the vault's voice-checked attributions. I'm attributing it from context, because he is addressing Bartlett.
- **His tiers of capital:** He ranks capital as friends and family, then institutional money, then public money. This ranking isn't on the vault's leverage page ([[business/leverage/types-of-leverage]]).

The underlying idea is Hormozi's, as the vault records it: identical work and skill earn very different amounts depending on the market, which he sums up as "same work more zeros". The NASDAQ valuation and the 7–8 million equity deal are Bartlett's biography. I'd keep them out of any summary of Hormozi's own history.

If you want the capital-tier remark and Bartlett's story captured properly, I can add them to the leverage page as a Hormozi statement plus a caveat that the anecdote is the host's.

**He didn't. The vault says the opposite.** In the one consult with a young roofing owner, Hormozi told him to go all in on door-to-door as his main growth channel. I searched the full transcript and the rest of the raw sources for Google Ads, paid search and "stop knocking". Google appears only in "you can google to verify" in his bio. The only ads he discusses elsewhere are Meta-style ad creative for other businesses.

**Based on:** said it. The source is the roofer's consult (Keys Roofing, owner Caleb, St. Louis) from the "Scale or Fail" series, 2026-08-29: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]], [[sales/outbound/door-to-door-canvassing]]).

**What he actually told him**
- "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 9:49, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s)
- "I think you building out this DDD army is like the clear straight shot." (@ 10:54; "DDD" is the auto-caption for D2D)
- Near the end he waves off the newer, more exciting options and sums up the plan: "But like we need to knock more doors" and "we sell more repairs." (@ 20:42)
- The 90-day recap puts it as: "the first thing we said was go all in on door to door as primary growth engine." (@ 24:27)

**Why he said it**
- **Reliability.** The owner said about 20 doors gets him one sale. Hormozi called that a rare asset: "that reliability of being able to just basically go get money um is something that a lot of entrepreneurs don't know how to do." (@ 3:16)
- **Highest return first.** "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." (@ 3:16) For a two-month-old company, door-knocking already worked and cost almost nothing.
- **Scale by hiring, not switching channels.** He wanted commission paid per door, so reps' income tracks effort: "how much money do you want to make? Just knock that many doors." (@ 10:54) The $10-per-door number is his illustration, not a measured figure.
- **It's what the owner is good at.** "It's what you're good at." (@ 10:21)

This fits his general rules. He fixes the channel that already works before adding a new one, saying "New channel, little too hard for right now in my opinion" in another consult ([[yt-MH-IMJxbUY4]] @ 24:06). He also says "no Hail Mary's. This is just consistent yardage" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 4:19).

**The rest of the consult:** more repairs than replacements, a VSL before the sale, a maintenance membership, the menu upsell and speed fees. None of it is Google Ads.

**Where the claim might come from:** you may be thinking of a different consult or a different video. If you saw it somewhere specific, tell me where and I'll check. Hormozi's usual advice would not conflict with ads later, once the owner has a proven offer. His ads advice is to keep spending while ROAS holds ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 10:48). The vault has nothing showing him telling this roofer to do that now.
